newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Italy, Austria call for sweeping EU rights clause.
newsitem.headline: Italy, Austria call for sweeping EU rights clause.

text.p: Italy and Austria called on Tuesday for a sweeping human rights clause to be incorporated in the European Union treaty and for the Union to be given the power to penalise member countries that do not comply.
The two countries also called for the EU as a body to sign up to the European Convention on Human Rights and to respect other international constitutional instruments.

At a joint news conference, Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini and Austrian Vice Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel said their proposal was designed to underline to citizens the benefits of being part of the Union.
"We feel that Europe must become a comprehensive and understandable process to the citizen," Schuessel said.
The proposal -- which will be presented to the inter-governmental conference (IGC) -- would prohibit discrimination across the EU on a broad range of grounds.
Article F (bis) would be added to read:

"The Union shall ensure that no discrimination on grounds particularly of race, colour, nationality, sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, association with a national minority, social origin or property, disability, sexual preference or any other specific status takes place."
It also formally pledged the Union to combatting "racism, anti-Semitism, xenophobia, intolerance, sexism and inclusion."

In what is likely to be among the most controversial aspects of the proposal, the two countries said any EU member that persistently breached any of these rights should, after due process among the Council and European Parliament, have certain benefits within the Union suspended.
"If a member state infringes such rights, then there must be penalties," Schuessel said.
The two countries said it was also important that the EU sign up to the Convention on Human Rights and that all EU laws should be completely accessible to the Union's citizens.
The European Court of Justice has ruled that the EU currently lacks the standing to accede as a body to the human rights convention.
